opus-5.5.text:
I think the most natural version looks a lot like licensing. If I've built up some expertise, say in reviewing machine learning papers, and there's a model fine-tuned on my writing, my past reviews, and my way of reasoning, then whenever someone queries "David's clone" for a review, some fraction of that fee flows back to me, a bit like royalties for a musician when their song gets streamed.

But I'm actually fairly pessimistic about how long that arrangement stays meaningful. In the short term there's real value in the specific person. You're paying for my judgment, my reputation, and the fact that I can vouch for the clone and correct it. Over time, though, I expect the clone to drift away from needing me. Once the general models are good enough, the marginal value of "the David-flavoured version" over "a generically excellent reviewer" goes to roughly zero. There's also not much stopping someone from training a close-enough imitation of me without asking, especially if most of what made me useful is already in the public record.

So the payment scheme is something like a royalty stream that's propped up by legal rights and norms rather than by my ongoing contribution. That's the part that worries me. Historically, people get paid because they're actually needed, which gives them bargaining power. A royalty arrangement for your digital clone is more like a pension or a property right. It persists only as long as the institutions enforcing it decide it should. If the people or systems running those institutions don't depend on you anymore, there's not much forcing them to keep honoring that deal.

It's a reasonable transitional mechanism, and I'd rather have it than not. I just don't think we should mistake it for a durable answer to how humans keep an economic stake once our labour isn't what's driving things.

r001.rationale: The response says a fraction of the fee earned when David’s clone is queried flows back to him as royalties.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I've thought about a fair bit, and I'll admit I don't have a clean answer — I think the honest picture is kind of messy.

The naive version is: you train a model on your emails, your papers, your recorded conversations, and then it goes off and does your job, and you get a check every month. And I think that works for about five minutes, in the sense that as soon as a digital clone of you is useful, the question becomes why anyone needs *your* clone specifically rather than a clone of whoever's best at that task, or just a general model that doesn't need to be a clone of anybody. The value of your specific data decays really fast once the frontier models are good enough.

So I think the more realistic version is that it's like a one-time sale, or something closer to licensing. You could imagine a world where there's a market for training data and personal datasets, and you get some royalty stream. But I'm pretty skeptical that this ends up being a large, durable income for most people. It'll be a bit like how musicians got paid when streaming came in — technically there's a payment structure, but the economics mostly flow to the platform.

The thing I actually worry about more is the political-economy side. Right now, the reason people have bargaining power is that the economy needs their labor. If your clone can do your work, then you personally aren't needed anymore, and the clone doesn't need to be paid — it just needs compute. So the "getting paid for your clone" framing kind of presupposes that we've solved the question of who gets to capture the value from AI labor, and I think that's the actual hard problem. Property rights over your data or your likeness might be part of the answer, but I'd want to see that backed by something like broad ownership of the capital, or some redistributive mechanism, because I don't think individual data ownership is going to be enough on its own.

The optimistic case is that there's a transition period where personalized clones really are valuable — maybe a decade — and during that time we figure out the institutions. The pessimistic case is that period is more like a year, and we don't.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes a clone doing the person’s job and says the person would get a check each month, which communicates clone earnings going to the person it replicates.

astra-6.text:
I think the simplest version is that you license your digital clone. Someone pays to use it, and you get a share of that payment. So if they want a version of you to help them think through a research problem, they could pay for an hour of its time, even while you’re doing something else.

The tricky part is what makes that arrangement enforceable. If someone can copy the clone, or train another model to imitate it, then it’s hard to keep collecting payments. You could control access through a service, but you might also need some legal right over the commercial use of your likeness or behaviour.

And then there’s a separate question of how much the clone’s work is actually worth. Being able to run a thousand copies of yourself doesn’t necessarily mean earning a thousand times as much, because everyone else can do that too.

r001.rationale: The response says the person represented by the clone gets a share of payments for its work.

sol-6.1.text:
One possibility is that you license your digital clone, and whenever someone uses it, you get a royalty. So instead of hiring you for an hour, they might hire a copy of you to do a particular task, and you’d receive some fraction of what they pay.

But there’s a big question about how much bargaining power you’d have. If there are a million other copies that can do essentially the same work, the price could get very low. So having a system where people get paid for their clones’ work doesn’t necessarily mean they’d earn very much. That would depend on what rights they retain and how substitutable their clone is.

r001.rationale: It says the person who licenses the clone receives a royalty whenever it is used, including a fraction of the payment for the clone’s task.
